_comment: Bundled vocabulary for the audit-pack validator (contract requirement 3).
Kept in sync with contract/audit-pack.schema.json by scripts/check_repo.py.
These are the SHAPES an audit workpaper takes — how a control was tested, what was inspected,
how a population was sampled, and what was done about each exception. They are not framework
content: no control text, no testing guidance, no evidence-item list. What is in scope, what
the framework expects and how an auditor tests it all come from the customer's own
organization at scan time. See contract/README.md, requirement 9.
The testing procedure in particular is deliberately absent. The queue snapshot records only
whether one is available; the text stays behind the API, where it belongs.
_sampling_method_comment: Two methods, both reproducible, and that is the whole reason there are only two. A sample this
piece records has to be one anybody can redraw from the population file, the seed and the size
— including the auditor, and including you in a year. A judgemental selection is a legitimate
audit technique and is not one of these: record it as full_population over the subset you
actually tested, and say in the rationale how the subset was chosen.
_minimum_sample_comment: The smallest defensible sample for a population of a given size, and a floor rather than a
recommendation: a sample below it is one an auditor will ask about, so the validator asks
first. Where the population is smaller than the floor, everything has to be tested.
Bands are read in order and the first whose `up_to` covers the population size wins; the last
band has `up_to: null` and covers everything above.
_assurance_days_comment: How long a conclusion about an audit window may stand, counted in days from the END of the
window it covers. A workpaper concludes about a period, so the period's end is the only honest
anchor: signing it late does not extend what it covers.
A finding of `effective` runs to roughly the next annual cycle. `deficient` and `not_tested`
get a short horizon on purpose — a control you found broken, or never tested, is not something
to sign off for a year and revisit at the next audit.
